verdict.rationale: Across the cited texts God or the Spirit is the grammatical agent of perception and teaching verbs, and the believer is the recipient. In 1 Cor 2:10 God revealed (apekalypsen, aorist active) the things through the Spirit, who searches (eraunai, present) the deep things of God; in v.12 we received the Spirit so that we may know (eidomen); in v.13 the words are Spirit-taught (didaktois pneumatos); in v.14 the natural person is not able to know (ou dynatai gnonai) because such things are spiritually examined (anakrinetai, present passive). John 16:13 has the Spirit guide (hodegesei, future) into all the truth, Eph 1:18 has the eyes of the heart enlightened (pephotismenous, perfect passive participle), Luke 24:45 has Christ open (dianoixen) the mind to understand the Scriptures, and Ps 119:18 petitions God to open (gal) the eyes to see wonders in the torah. The pattern spans law and writings, prophecy, gospel, and epistle. The genuine open question the words leave is scope, whether this illumination adds new content or grants understanding of the already given word, and whether the all in all the truth is exhaustive or apostolic, but no reading reverses the core claim that the Spirit gives believers spiritual understanding of God's word.

scripture.force: God revealed (apekalypsen, V-AAI-3S aorist active indicative) these things to us through the Spirit (dia tou pneumatos), and the Spirit searches (eraunai, V-PAI-3S present active) all things, even the deep things (ta bathe) of God. The morphology fixes God as the subject who reveals and the Spirit as the searching agent, with believers as recipients in the dative hemin. Revelatory and investigative action is bound to the divine Spirit.

As no one knows (egnoken, V-RAI-3S perfect) the things of a man except the man's own spirit, so no one has known (egnoken) the things of God except the Spirit of God. The analogy grounds the claim that only the divine Spirit possesses inside knowledge of God, which is why Spirit-given access is required for others to know.

We received (elabomen, aorist) the Spirit who is from God (to ek tou theou), expressed in a purpose clause hina eidomen (V-RAS-1P) so that we may know the things freely given (charisthenta) to us by God. Knowing the gifted truths of God is grammatically conditioned on receiving the divine Spirit.

We speak these things not in words taught by human wisdom (didaktois anthropines sophias) but in words taught by the Spirit (didaktois pneumatos), interpreting spiritual things to spiritual people (pneumatikois pneumatika synkrinontes). The verbal adjective didaktos with the genitive pneumatos makes the Spirit the explicit source of the instruction. didaktos is a near hapax, three tokens in two verses, but the parallel didaktois anthropines sophias inside the same clause disambiguates its sense by direct antithesis.

The natural person (psychikos anthropos) does not receive (ou dechetai, V-PNI-3S) the things of the Spirit of God, for they are foolishness to him, and he is not able to know them (ou dynatai gnonai, V-2AAN) because they are spiritually examined (pneumatikos anakrinetai, V-PPI-3S present passive). The present passive of anakrino plus the modal ou dynatai grammatically forecloses the natural faculty and makes Spirit-given discernment the necessary condition for apprehending God's word.

Who has known (egno, aorist) the mind of the Lord (noun kyriou) so as to instruct him, but we have the mind of Christ (noun Christou echomen, V-PAI-1P). The argument closes by giving believers the noun Christou, the cognitive faculty that the natural person of v.14 lacked, completing the contrast.

The anointing (chrisma) which you received from him remains (menei) in you, and you have no need that anyone teach you (ou chreian echete hina tis didaske hymas, present subjunctive), but as his anointing teaches you (didaskei hymas, V-PAI-3S present) concerning all things and is true and is not a lie. chrisma occurs only here and in v.20, a hapax cluster confined to 1 John, but didasko in the present indicative names the teaching action plainly. The clause about needing no human teacher reads in context against the deceivers of vv.18 to 26.

When the Spirit of truth (to pneuma tes aletheias) comes, he will guide you (hodegesei hymas, V-FAI-3S future) into all the truth (eis ten aletheian pasan), for he will not speak from himself, but whatever he hears he will speak, and he will announce (anangelei, V-FAI-3S future) to you the things that are coming (ta erchomena). hodegeo elsewhere is literal leading of the blind (Matt 15:14, Luke 6:39), so the sense here is metaphorical leading into comprehension. The future tense and the second person plural leave open whether all the truth is exhaustive or bounded to the apostolic circle being addressed.

The Paraclete (ho parakletos), the Holy Spirit whom the Father will send in my name, that one will teach you all things (didaxei hymas panta, V-FAI-3S future) and will remind you (hypomnesei) of all that I said to you. The Spirit's teaching office toward the disciples is explicit, paired with reminding of already spoken words.

Paul prays that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ may give (doe, optative) to you a spirit of wisdom and revelation (pneuma sophias kai apokalypseos) in the knowledge (en epignosei) of him. The wisdom and revelatory faculty for knowing God is requested as a gift, with pneuma, sophia, and apokalypsis clustered, echoing the ruach chokmah of Isa 11:2.

The eyes of your heart having been enlightened (pephotismenous, V-RPP-APM perfect passive participle) for you to know (eis to eidenai, perfect infinitive) what is the hope of his calling and the riches of his inheritance. The perfect passive of photizo names a completed illumination wrought upon the believer, and the purpose is comprehension of what is already declared. The object here is understanding of given content, not new content.

Then he opened (dienoixen, V-AAI-3S aorist active) their mind (ton noun) so as to understand the Scriptures (tou synienai tas graphas). Here the object of the opening is explicitly the written graphas, and the agent is Christ acting on the disciples' noun. This is the clearest text tying divinely given understanding directly to comprehension of the existing word.

Open (gal, imperative of galah, uncover) my eyes (enay) that I may behold (we-abbitah, from nabat) wonders (niphlaot) out of your law (mi-toratecha). The psalmist petitions God to open his eyes for perception of wonders that are already in the written torah. The agent of opening is God, the recipient is the worshiper, and the object of sight is the existing word, a direct OT prototype of the illumination pattern.

The Spirit of the LORD (ruach YHWH) will rest on him, a Spirit of wisdom and understanding (ruach chokmah u-binah), of counsel and might, of knowledge and the fear of the LORD. The fourfold ruach plus cognitive nouns chokmah, binah, and daat is the OT pattern that links the Spirit to wisdom and understanding, the same cluster Eph 1:17 echoes with pneuma sophias.

complicating_texts.resolution: The clause ou chreian echete hina tis didaske hymas, you have no need that anyone teach you, could be read to abolish ordinary instruction and so over-prove the case into anti-teaching. The present subjunctive and the immediate context resolve it. John writes this against the deceivers, the antichristoi of vv.18 to 26, so the contrast is the Spirit's protective discernment versus seducers, not the Spirit versus all teachers. The anointing's didactic role is the safeguarding knowledge the Spirit gives, which is consistent with the broader illumination pattern, not against it.

hodegesei hymas eis ten aletheian pasan with the future tense and second person plural is spoken to the upper-room circle, raising whether guide into all the truth extends to ordinary believers or is a bounded apostolic promise, especially given anangelei ta erchomena, announce the coming things. This is a genuine scope question the words do not settle. It does not unseat the verdict, because the same Spirit-and-knowing cluster recurs in 1 Cor 2:10 to 16, 1 John 2:27, and Eph 1:17 to 18, all addressed to general readerships, carrying the illumination of believers regardless of how the maximal apostolic reading of this single verse resolves.

psychikos anthropos ou dechetai and ou dynatai gnonai could be read to deny any natural cognitive grasp of the text at all, which would prove too much, since unbelievers plainly can parse the words on a page. anakrinetai is present passive and the verbs dechomai and ginosko here concern reception and salvific apprehension, the spiritual discernment of v.15, not bare literacy. So the verse marks the faculty needed for spiritual apprehension, which is exactly the Spirit-given understanding the proposition asserts.

The revelatory weight of anangelei ta erchomena and the apokalypto and apokalypsis vocabulary raises a second scope question, whether illumination conveys genuinely new content or grants understanding of the already given word. The lexicon carries both senses. Eph 1:18 photizo and Luke 24:45 dianoigo plus Ps 119:18 gal point to understanding of existing content, while apokalypto and anangello can denote fresh disclosure. The words do not rank these, so the verdict affirms the core claim while leaving this content-versus-understanding scope underdetermined, which is why divergence among readers is lexically explicable.

variant_units_examined.note: The conjunction at the head of v.10, de versus gar across witnesses, does not touch the revelatory verb apekalypsen or its agent ho theos dia tou pneumatos. Not in the ingested ECM window, assessed from morphology only.
Whether the genitive reads pneumatos or hagiou pneumatos in didaktois pneumatos is a stylistic expansion. The Spirit-taught-words clause and its sense are stable. Not in ECM scope.
The indicative menete versus imperative reading and the menei variant of meno affect mood, not the didactic action of the chrisma, which is the verb didaskei. Not in ECM scope.

variants.note: No cited verse falls in the ingested ECM window, which is 3 John 1.1 to 1.15, so variants here are assessed from morphology and known apparatus signals rather than CBGM. The examined units are stylistic and do not unseat the lexical pattern.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: The perception and teaching verbs, apokalypto aorist active, eraunao present, didasko, hodegeo future, photizo perfect passive, and dianoigo aorist, place the action with God or the Spirit and the believer as recipient in the dative and accusative pronouns. The psychikos versus pneumatikos contrast in 1 Cor 2:14 to 15 grammatically forecloses the natural faculty, so the text affirms Spirit-given spiritual understanding.

The OT pattern of the ruach of wisdom and understanding in Isa 11:2 and the petition to have the eyes opened to the torah in Ps 119:18 carry forward into the Paraclete's teaching office in John 14 and 16 and the apostolic letters, showing one covenantal arc in which the Spirit leads God's people into the truth of the word.

On the reading that the Spirit's office is to grant understanding of the already given word rather than to add new content, Eph 1:18 enlightens the eyes to know what is declared, Luke 24:45 opens the mind to understand the existing Scriptures, and Ps 119:18 asks for sight of wonders already in the torah. This lens affirms the proposition directly and reads it as illumination of Scripture in the strict sense.

On the reading that the cluster is primarily revelatory, apokalypto and apokalypsis in 1 Cor 2:10 and Eph 1:17 and anangelei ta erchomena in John 16:13 denote fresh disclosure rather than mere comprehension of prior text. This lens still affirms the proposition, since the Spirit is the agent giving believers understanding of God's truth, but it reads the scope as broader than the written word alone.

Read strongly, John 16:13 hodegesei hymas eis ten aletheian pasan is a promise to the apostolic circle that grounds the foundational deposit of truth, with the announcing of coming things as a special office. On this lens the verse itself is bounded, yet the proposition still stands for all believers because 1 Cor 2, 1 John 2:27, and Eph 1:17 to 18 address general readerships and supply the believer-wide illumination.

hermeneutics.notes: There is no lexical conflict over whether the Spirit gives understanding, every lens affirms that. The genuine divergence among readers is over scope, content versus understanding and apostolic versus all-believer, and the vocabulary underdetermines both. progressive_revelation is marked true because the verdict traces an OT to NT arc from the ruach of wisdom and the opened eyes upon the torah to the Paraclete and the apostolic letters.

stem_audit.notes: The stem uses illumine, Spirit, Scripture, and spiritual understanding, which are biblical and descriptive vocabulary. The claim does not encode a tradition-specific taxonomy or smuggle its own conclusion, so the verdict is derived from the lexical data on the original stem. The cross-references cited in the prior evidence file were labeled source tsk but the actual store relationship for those exact verse pairs is OPENBIBLE_CROSS_REF from OpenBible-cross-refs, so the source label and vote counts have been corrected to openbible against queried data. This is a data-integrity fix and does not change the verdict.

lay_summary: Across the cited passages the words used for what God and the Spirit do line up cleanly with the proposition, and the grammar makes the picture firm. In 1 Corinthians 2:10 God revealed (apekalypsen) these things through the Spirit, who searches (eraunai) even the deep things of God. Verse 12 says believers received the Spirit so that they may know the things freely given, and verse 13 says the words are taught by the Spirit (didaktois pneumatos). Verse 14 says the natural person is not able to know them because they are spiritually examined (anakrinetai, a passive form), and verse 16 says believers have the mind of Christ. John 16:13 says the Spirit will guide (hodegesei) into all the truth, John 14:26 that he will teach all things, Ephesians 1:18 that the eyes of the heart are enlightened (pephotismenous) to know what is already declared, and Luke 24:45 that Christ opened the mind to understand the Scriptures. Psalm 119:18 asks God to open (gal) the eyes to see wonders in his written law. The agent is always God or the Spirit, the recipient is the believer, and the object is the truth of God including the written word, and the pattern runs from the Old Testament psalm and prophecy through the gospels into the letters, so the confidence is high. Where careful readers diverge is only about scope, and that divergence comes from the words themselves. Some terms, like reveal and announce the coming things, can mean brand new content, while others, like enlighten the eyes and open the mind to understand the Scriptures, clearly mean grasping what is already given, and the vocabulary does not rank which is primary. Likewise the promise to guide into all the truth is spoken to a small group, so the words leave open whether all the truth is everything or the apostolic deposit. None of these open questions reverses the core claim that the Spirit gives believers spiritual understanding of God's word.
